**Aaron Douglas** (May 26, 1899 – February 2, 1979[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1)) was an [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") painter, illustrator, and [visual arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_arts "Visual arts") educator. He was a major figure in the [Harlem Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Renaissance "Harlem Renaissance").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2) He developed his art career painting [murals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural "Mural") and creating illustrations that addressed social issues around race and [segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States "Racial segregation in the United States") in the United States by utilizing African-centric imagery.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3) Douglas set the stage for young, African-American artists to enter the public-arts realm through his involvement with the [Harlem Artists Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Artists_Guild "Harlem Artists Guild").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:3-4) In 1944, he concluded his art career by founding the Art Department at [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University") in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee"). He taught visual art classes at Fisk University until his retirement in 1966.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) Douglas is known as a prominent leader in modern African-American art whose work influenced artists for years to come.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Aaron Douglas was born and raised in [Topeka, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topeka,_Kansas "Topeka, Kansas"), on May 26, 1899,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) to Aaron Douglas Sr, a baker from [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"), and Elizabeth Douglas, a homemaker and amateur artist from [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"). His passion for art derived from admiring his mother's drawings.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He attended [Topeka High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topeka_High_School "Topeka High School"), during which he worked for Skinner's Nursery and [Union Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad "Union Pacific Railroad") material yard, and graduated in 1917.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-7)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3)

After high school, Douglas moved to Detroit, Michigan, and held various jobs, including working as a plasterer and molding sand for automobile radiators at the Cadillac factory. During this time, he attended free classes at the Detroit Museum of Art. Douglas travelled further eastward, through East St. Louis to Dunkirk in upstate New York, working at the Essex Glass factory to earn money for college. He went on to attend college at the [University of Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nebraska%E2%80%93Lincoln "University of Nebraska–Lincoln") in 1918.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) While there, Douglas worked as a busboy to finance his education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) When the United States entered [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), Douglas attempted to join the [Student Army Training Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_Army_Training_Corps "Student Army Training Corps") (SATC) at the University of Nebraska, but was dismissed. Historians have speculated that this dismissal was related to the racially segregated climate of American society and the military.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) He then transferred for a short time to the [University of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota"), where he volunteered for the SATC and attained the rank of corporal. After the signing of [the armistice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_11_November_1918 "Armistice of 11 November 1918"), he returned to the University of Nebraska,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) where he received a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in 1922.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8)

After graduating, Douglas worked as a waiter for the [Union Pacific Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad "Union Pacific Railroad") until 1923, when he secured a job teaching visual arts at [Lincoln High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_High_School_(Kansas_City,_Missouri) "Lincoln High School (Kansas City, Missouri)") in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), staying there until 1925. During his time in Kansas City, he exchanged letters with Alta Sawyer, his future wife, about his plans beyond teaching in a high-school setting. He wanted to take his art career to [Paris, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_France "Paris, France"), as many of his aspiring artist peers did.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1925–27

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1925–27")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/FireFrontCover.webp/250px-FireFrontCover.webp?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FireFrontCover.webp)

The cover of the first and only issue of the magazine _Fire!!_ (1926) was designed by Aaron Douglas.

In 1925, Douglas intended to pass through [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"), New York, on his way to Paris to advance his art career.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He was convinced to stay in Harlem and develop his art during the height of the [Harlem Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Renaissance "Harlem Renaissance"), influenced by the writings of [Alain Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Locke "Alain Locke") about the importance of Harlem for aspiring African Americans.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3) While in Harlem, Douglas studied under [Winold Reiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winold_Reiss "Winold Reiss"), a German portraitist who encouraged him to work with African-centric themes to create a sense of unity between African Americans with art;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) Douglas was included in Alain Locke's 1925 anthology _[The New Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Negro "The New Negro")_ as Reiss's pupil.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

Douglas worked with [W. E. B. Du Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois "W. E. B. Du Bois"), then-editor at _[The Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crisis "The Crisis")_, a monthly journal of the [NAACP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People "National Association for the Advancement of Colored People"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2) and became art editor himself briefly in 1927.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10) Douglas also illustrated for [Charles S. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_S._Johnson "Charles S. Johnson"), then-editor at _[Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity:\_A\_Journal\_of\_Negro\_Life "Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life")_, the official publication of the [National Urban League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Urban_League "National Urban League").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2) These illustrations focused on articles about [lynching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching "Lynching") and [segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segregation_in_the_United_States "Segregation in the United States"), and theater and jazz.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10) His illustrations also featured in the periodicals _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity\_Fair\_(magazine) "Vanity Fair (magazine)")_ and _[Theatre Arts Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre\_Arts\_Monthly "Theatre Arts Monthly")_ and made the cover of the only issue of the African-American avantgarde magazine _[Fire!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire!! "Fire!!")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:12-11) In 1927, Douglas was asked to create the first of his murals at Club Ebony, which highlighted Harlem nightlife.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12)

### 1928–31

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1928–31")]

In 1928, Douglas received a one-year [Barnes Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnes_Foundation "Barnes Foundation") Fellowship in [Philadelphia, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia,_Pennsylvania "Philadelphia, Pennsylvania"), where [Albert C. Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_C._Barnes "Albert C. Barnes"), philanthropist and founder of the Barnes Foundation, supported him in studying the collection of Modernist paintings and African art.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) During this same year, Douglas participated in the [Harmon Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_E._Harmon_Foundation "William E. Harmon Foundation")'s exhibition organized by the [College Art Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Art_Association "College Art Association"), entitled "Contemporary Negro Art."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) In the summer of 1930, he moved to Nashville, Tennessee, where he worked on a series of murals for [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University")'s Cravath Hall library that he described as a "panorama of the development of Black people in this hemisphere, in the new world."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-13) While in Nashville, he was commissioned by the [Sherman Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman_House_Hotel "Sherman House Hotel") in [Chicago, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois"), to paint a mural series. In addition, he was commissioned by [Bennett College for Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_College_for_Women "Bennett College for Women") in [Greensboro, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro,_North_Carolina "Greensboro, North Carolina"), to create a mural with [Harriet Tubman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Tubman "Harriet Tubman") as its primary figure.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He then moved in 1931 for one year to Paris, France, where he received training in sculpture and painting at the Académie Scandinave.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

### 1934–36

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1934–36")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/75/Into_Bondage_Douglas_1936.jpg/250px-Into_Bondage_Douglas_1936.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Into_Bondage_Douglas_1936.jpg)

_Into Bondage_ (1936) at the [National Gallery of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Art "National Gallery of Art") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), in 2022.

Douglas returned to Harlem in the mid-1930s to work on his mural painting techniques. Having joined the American Communist Party at some point upon return, he began to explore more political topics within his art as well.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) In 1934, he was commissioned by New York's [135th Street YMCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_YMCA "Harlem YMCA") to paint a mural on their building, as well as by the [Public Works Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Works_Administration "Public Works Administration") to paint his most acclaimed mural cycle, _Aspects of Negro Life,_ for the [Countee Cullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countee_Cullen "Countee Cullen") Branch of [New York Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) He used these murals to inform his audiences of the place of African Americans throughout America's history and its present society.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) In a series consisting of four murals, Douglas takes his audience from an African setting, to [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") and the [Reconstruction era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_Era "Reconstruction Era") in the United States, then through the threats of lynching and segregation in a post-Civil War America to a final mural depicting the movement of African Americans north towards the Harlem Renaissance and the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States "Great Depression in the United States").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12) Douglas created a similar series of murals, which included _Into Bondage_ (1936), for the Texas Centennial Exposition in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas") in 1936.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-NGA_listing-14)

During the height of his commissioned work as a muralist, Douglas served as president of the [Harlem Artists Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Artists_Guild "Harlem Artists Guild") in 1935, an organization designed to create a network of young artists in New York City to provide support, inspiration, and to help out young artists during the Harlem Renaissance.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:3-4)

### 1937–66

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1937–66")]

In 1937, the [Rosenwald Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosenwald_Foundation "Rosenwald Foundation") awarded Douglas a travel fellowship to go to the American South and visit primarily [Black universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges_and_universities "Historically black colleges and universities"), including [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University") in Nashville, Tennessee, the [Tuskegee Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_Institute "Tuskegee Institute") in Alabama, and [Dillard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dillard_University "Dillard University") in [New Orleans, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans,_Louisiana "New Orleans, Louisiana"). In 1938, he again received a travel fellowship from the Rosenwald Foundation to go to the [Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic") and [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti") to develop a series of watercolors depicting the life of these Caribbean islands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)

Upon returning to the United States in 1940, he worked at Fisk University in Nashville, while attending [Columbia University Teacher’s College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_Teacher%E2%80%99s_College "Columbia University Teacher’s College") in New York City. He received his Master of Arts degree in 1944, and moved to Nashville, to found and sit as the chairman of the Art Department at Fisk.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) During his tenure as a professor in the Art Department, he was the founding director of the Carl Van Vechten Gallery of Fine Arts, which included both White and African-American art in an effort to educate students on being an artist in a segregated American South.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1) Douglas used his experiences as an artist in the Harlem Renaissance to inspire his students to expand on the movements of African-American art. He also encouraged his students to study African-American history to fully understand the necessity for African-American art in predominantly White-American society.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) Douglas retired from teaching in the Art Department at Fisk University in 1966.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

### 1967–79

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1967–79")]

Aaron Douglas died in Nashville on February 2, 1979, at the age of 79.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Aaron_Douglas_by_Edwin_Harleston_%2851419%29.jpg/250px-Aaron_Douglas_by_Edwin_Harleston_%2851419%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aaron_Douglas_by_Edwin_Harleston_(51419).jpg)

Portrait of Douglas by [Edwin Harleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Harleston "Edwin Harleston") (1930), featured in the _Harlem Renaissance and Transatlantic Modernism_ exhibition at the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art")

Aaron Douglas pioneered the African-American modernist movement by combining aesthetic with ancient African traditional art. He set the stage for future African-American artists to utilize elements of African and African-American history alongside racial themes present in society.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:12-11)

In 2007, the [Spencer Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Museum_of_Art "Spencer Museum of Art") organized an exhibition titled _Aaron Douglas: African-American Modernist_. It was held in [Lawrence, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Kansas "Lawrence, Kansas"), at the Spencer Museum of Art between September 8 to December 2, 2007, and traveled to the [Frist Center for the Visual Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frist_Center_for_the_Visual_Arts "Frist Center for the Visual Arts") in Nashville, Tennessee, from January 18 to April 13, 2008. It was then on display at the [Smithsonian American Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_American_Art_Museum "Smithsonian American Art Museum") in Washington, D.C,. between May 9 and August 3, 2008. Finally, it traveled to the [Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schomburg_Center_for_Research_in_Black_Culture "Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture") in New York, New York, from August 30 to November 30, 2008. An exhaustive catalog of this exhibition was put together through collaboration between Spencer Museum of Art and [The University of Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kansas "University of Kansas"), with the title _Aaron Douglas: African American Modernist_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:2-15)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-16)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1)

Douglas's work was featured in the 2015 exhibition _[We Speak: Black Artists in Philadelphia, 1920s-1970s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We\_Speak:\_Black\_Artists\_in\_Philadelphia,\_1920s-1970s "We Speak: Black Artists in Philadelphia, 1920s-1970s")_ at the [Woodmere Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodmere_Art_Museum "Woodmere Art Museum").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-Woodmere_Art_Museum-17)

In 2016, with the opening of the [National Museum of African American History and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_American_History_and_Culture "National Museum of African American History and Culture"), an archive of artworks created by or having to do with Aaron Douglas became available on their website. Users can access the full references of these pieces of art to determine the creation date, subject of the art, and its current residence.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-18)

## Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Style")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/4a/Lagos%2C_Nigeria_by_Aaron_Douglas.jpg/250px-Lagos%2C_Nigeria_by_Aaron_Douglas.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lagos,_Nigeria_by_Aaron_Douglas.jpg)

_Lagos, Nigeria_ (1956)

Aaron Douglas developed two art styles during his career: first as a traditional [portraitist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait "Portrait"), then as a [muralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural "Mural") and [illustrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustrator "Illustrator").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1) Influenced by having worked with [Winold Reiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winold_Reiss "Winold Reiss"), Douglas incorporated African themes into his artwork to create a connection between Africans and African Americans. His work is described as being abstract, in that he portrayed the universality of the African-American people through song, dance, imagery and poetry.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) Through his murals and illustrations for various publications, he addressed social issues connected with race and segregation in the United States, and was one of the first African-American visual artists to utilize African-centered imagery.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3)

His work features silhouettes of men and women, often in black and white.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8) His human depictions have characteristically flat shapes that are angular and long, with slits for eyes. Often, his female figures are drawn in a crouched position or moving as if they are dancing in a traditional African way.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) He adopted elements of West African masks and sculptures into his own art,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:12-11) with a technique that utilized [cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism") to simplify his figures into lines and planes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He employed a narrow range of color, tone and value, most often using greens, browns, mauves, and blacks, with his human forms in darker shades of the present colors of the painting. He created emotional impact with subtle gradations of color, often using concentric circles to influence the viewer to focus on a specific part of the painting.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9)

His artwork is two-dimensional, and his human figures are faceless, allowing their forms to be symbolic and general, so as to create a sense of unity between Africans and African Americans.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) Douglas’ paintings include semitransparent silhouettes to portray the struggle of African Americans and their relative successes in various aspects of social life.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8) His work is described as unique in creating a link between African Americans and their African ancestry through visual elements that are rooted in African art, and thus give the African-American experience a symbolic aesthetic.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12)

*   Illustrations for [Paul Morand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Morand "Paul Morand"), _Black Magic_, 1929[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:2-15)
*   _Harriet Tubman_, mural at [Bennett College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_College "Bennett College"), 1930[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:2-15)
*   _Symbolic Negro History_, murals at Fisk University, 1930[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)
*   _Dance Magic_, murals for the Sherman Hotel, Chicago, 1930–31[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3)
*   Series of illustrations and later paintings initially created for [James Weldon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Weldon_Johnson "James Weldon Johnson")’s _God’s Trombones: Seven Negro Sermons in Verse_[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:1-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-20)
    *   _Let My People Go_, circa 1935–39
    *   _The Judgment Day_, created in 1939

*   Mural series commissioned in 1934 by the [Works Progress Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Works_Progress_Administration "Works Progress Administration").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12) The series consists of four murals; 
    *   _The Negro in an African Setting,_ depicts elements of African cultural dances and music to highlight the central heritage of African Americans.
    *   _Slavery through Reconstruction,_ depicts the contrast between the promise of emancipation and political shift in power post-Civil War and the disappointments of Reconstruction in the United States.
    *   _The Idyll of the Deep South,_ depicts the perseverance of African-American song and dance against the cruelty of lynching and other threats to African Americans in the United States.
    *   _Song of the Towers,_ depicts three events in United States history from an African-American lens, including the movement of African Americans towards the North in the 1910s, the rise of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, and the Great Depression in the 1930s.

*   Four-part mural cycle (including _Aspiration_) at the [Texas Centennial Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Centennial_Exposition "Texas Centennial Exposition"), 1936[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-21)
*   Illustrations included in selected editions of [Countee Cullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countee_Cullen "Countee Cullen")'s _[Caroling Dusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroling\_Dusk "Caroling Dusk")_ and Alain Locke's _[The New Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Negro "The New Negro")_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:2-15)

American painter (1899–1979)

**Aaron Douglas** (May 26, 1899 – February 2, 1979[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1)) was an [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") painter, illustrator, and [visual arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_arts "Visual arts") educator. He was a major figure in the [Harlem Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Renaissance "Harlem Renaissance").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2) He developed his art career painting [murals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural "Mural") and creating illustrations that addressed social issues around race and [segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States "Racial segregation in the United States") in the United States by utilizing African-centric imagery.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3) Douglas set the stage for young, African-American artists to enter the public-arts realm through his involvement with the [Harlem Artists Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Artists_Guild "Harlem Artists Guild").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:3-4) In 1944, he concluded his art career by founding the Art Department at [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University") in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee"). He taught visual art classes at Fisk University until his retirement in 1966.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) Douglas is known as a prominent leader in modern African-American art whose work influenced artists for years to come.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Aaron Douglas was born and raised in [Topeka, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topeka,_Kansas "Topeka, Kansas"), on May 26, 1899,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) to Aaron Douglas Sr, a baker from [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"), and Elizabeth Douglas, a homemaker and amateur artist from [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama"). His passion for art derived from admiring his mother's drawings.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He attended [Topeka High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topeka_High_School "Topeka High School"), during which he worked for Skinner's Nursery and [Union Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad "Union Pacific Railroad") material yard, and graduated in 1917.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-7)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3)

After high school, Douglas moved to Detroit, Michigan, and held various jobs, including working as a plasterer and molding sand for automobile radiators at the Cadillac factory. During this time, he attended free classes at the Detroit Museum of Art. Douglas travelled further eastward, through East St. Louis to Dunkirk in upstate New York, working at the Essex Glass factory to earn money for college. He went on to attend college at the [University of Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nebraska%E2%80%93Lincoln "University of Nebraska–Lincoln") in 1918.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) While there, Douglas worked as a busboy to finance his education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) When the United States entered [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), Douglas attempted to join the [Student Army Training Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_Army_Training_Corps "Student Army Training Corps") (SATC) at the University of Nebraska, but was dismissed. Historians have speculated that this dismissal was related to the racially segregated climate of American society and the military.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) He then transferred for a short time to the [University of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota"), where he volunteered for the SATC and attained the rank of corporal. After the signing of [the armistice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_11_November_1918 "Armistice of 11 November 1918"), he returned to the University of Nebraska,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) where he received a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in 1922.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8)

After graduating, Douglas worked as a waiter for the [Union Pacific Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad "Union Pacific Railroad") until 1923, when he secured a job teaching visual arts at [Lincoln High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_High_School_(Kansas_City,_Missouri) "Lincoln High School (Kansas City, Missouri)") in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), staying there until 1925. During his time in Kansas City, he exchanged letters with Alta Sawyer, his future wife, about his plans beyond teaching in a high-school setting. He wanted to take his art career to [Paris, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_France "Paris, France"), as many of his aspiring artist peers did.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1925–27

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1925–27")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/FireFrontCover.webp/250px-FireFrontCover.webp?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FireFrontCover.webp)

The cover of the first and only issue of the magazine _Fire!!_ (1926) was designed by Aaron Douglas.

In 1925, Douglas intended to pass through [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"), New York, on his way to Paris to advance his art career.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He was convinced to stay in Harlem and develop his art during the height of the [Harlem Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Renaissance "Harlem Renaissance"), influenced by the writings of [Alain Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Locke "Alain Locke") about the importance of Harlem for aspiring African Americans.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3) While in Harlem, Douglas studied under [Winold Reiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winold_Reiss "Winold Reiss"), a German portraitist who encouraged him to work with African-centric themes to create a sense of unity between African Americans with art;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) Douglas was included in Alain Locke's 1925 anthology _[The New Negro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Negro "The New Negro")_ as Reiss's pupil.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

Douglas worked with [W. E. B. Du Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois "W. E. B. Du Bois"), then-editor at _[The Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crisis "The Crisis")_, a monthly journal of the [NAACP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People "National Association for the Advancement of Colored People"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2) and became art editor himself briefly in 1927.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10) Douglas also illustrated for [Charles S. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_S._Johnson "Charles S. Johnson"), then-editor at _[Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity:\_A\_Journal\_of\_Negro\_Life "Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life")_, the official publication of the [National Urban League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Urban_League "National Urban League").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:7-2) These illustrations focused on articles about [lynching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching "Lynching") and [segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segregation_in_the_United_States "Segregation in the United States"), and theater and jazz.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10) His illustrations also featured in the periodicals _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity\_Fair\_(magazine) "Vanity Fair (magazine)")_ and _[Theatre Arts Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre\_Arts\_Monthly "Theatre Arts Monthly")_ and made the cover of the only issue of the African-American avantgarde magazine _[Fire!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire!! "Fire!!")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:12-11) In 1927, Douglas was asked to create the first of his murals at Club Ebony, which highlighted Harlem nightlife.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12)

### 1928–31

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1928–31")]

In 1928, Douglas received a one-year [Barnes Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnes_Foundation "Barnes Foundation") Fellowship in [Philadelphia, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia,_Pennsylvania "Philadelphia, Pennsylvania"), where [Albert C. Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_C._Barnes "Albert C. Barnes"), philanthropist and founder of the Barnes Foundation, supported him in studying the collection of Modernist paintings and African art.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) During this same year, Douglas participated in the [Harmon Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_E._Harmon_Foundation "William E. Harmon Foundation")'s exhibition organized by the [College Art Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Art_Association "College Art Association"), entitled "Contemporary Negro Art."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) In the summer of 1930, he moved to Nashville, Tennessee, where he worked on a series of murals for [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University")'s Cravath Hall library that he described as a "panorama of the development of Black people in this hemisphere, in the new world."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-13) While in Nashville, he was commissioned by the [Sherman Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman_House_Hotel "Sherman House Hotel") in [Chicago, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois"), to paint a mural series. In addition, he was commissioned by [Bennett College for Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_College_for_Women "Bennett College for Women") in [Greensboro, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro,_North_Carolina "Greensboro, North Carolina"), to create a mural with [Harriet Tubman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Tubman "Harriet Tubman") as its primary figure.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He then moved in 1931 for one year to Paris, France, where he received training in sculpture and painting at the Académie Scandinave.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

### 1934–36

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1934–36")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/75/Into_Bondage_Douglas_1936.jpg/250px-Into_Bondage_Douglas_1936.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Into_Bondage_Douglas_1936.jpg)

_Into Bondage_ (1936) at the [National Gallery of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Art "National Gallery of Art") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), in 2022.

Douglas returned to Harlem in the mid-1930s to work on his mural painting techniques. Having joined the American Communist Party at some point upon return, he began to explore more political topics within his art as well.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) In 1934, he was commissioned by New York's [135th Street YMCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_YMCA "Harlem YMCA") to paint a mural on their building, as well as by the [Public Works Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Works_Administration "Public Works Administration") to paint his most acclaimed mural cycle, _Aspects of Negro Life,_ for the [Countee Cullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countee_Cullen "Countee Cullen") Branch of [New York Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) He used these murals to inform his audiences of the place of African Americans throughout America's history and its present society.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) In a series consisting of four murals, Douglas takes his audience from an African setting, to [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") and the [Reconstruction era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_Era "Reconstruction Era") in the United States, then through the threats of lynching and segregation in a post-Civil War America to a final mural depicting the movement of African Americans north towards the Harlem Renaissance and the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States "Great Depression in the United States").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12) Douglas created a similar series of murals, which included _Into Bondage_ (1936), for the Texas Centennial Exposition in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas") in 1936.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-NGA_listing-14)

During the height of his commissioned work as a muralist, Douglas served as president of the [Harlem Artists Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Artists_Guild "Harlem Artists Guild") in 1935, an organization designed to create a network of young artists in New York City to provide support, inspiration, and to help out young artists during the Harlem Renaissance.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:3-4)

### 1937–66

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1937–66")]

In 1937, the [Rosenwald Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosenwald_Foundation "Rosenwald Foundation") awarded Douglas a travel fellowship to go to the American South and visit primarily [Black universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges_and_universities "Historically black colleges and universities"), including [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University") in Nashville, Tennessee, the [Tuskegee Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskegee_Institute "Tuskegee Institute") in Alabama, and [Dillard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dillard_University "Dillard University") in [New Orleans, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans,_Louisiana "New Orleans, Louisiana"). In 1938, he again received a travel fellowship from the Rosenwald Foundation to go to the [Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic") and [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti") to develop a series of watercolors depicting the life of these Caribbean islands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6)

Upon returning to the United States in 1940, he worked at Fisk University in Nashville, while attending [Columbia University Teacher’s College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_Teacher%E2%80%99s_College "Columbia University Teacher’s College") in New York City. He received his Master of Arts degree in 1944, and moved to Nashville, to found and sit as the chairman of the Art Department at Fisk.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5) During his tenure as a professor in the Art Department, he was the founding director of the Carl Van Vechten Gallery of Fine Arts, which included both White and African-American art in an effort to educate students on being an artist in a segregated American South.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1) Douglas used his experiences as an artist in the Harlem Renaissance to inspire his students to expand on the movements of African-American art. He also encouraged his students to study African-American history to fully understand the necessity for African-American art in predominantly White-American society.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) Douglas retired from teaching in the Art Department at Fisk University in 1966.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

### 1967–79

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1967–79")]

Aaron Douglas died in Nashville on February 2, 1979, at the age of 79.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:4-5)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Aaron_Douglas_by_Edwin_Harleston_%2851419%29.jpg/250px-Aaron_Douglas_by_Edwin_Harleston_%2851419%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aaron_Douglas_by_Edwin_Harleston_(51419).jpg)

Portrait of Douglas by [Edwin Harleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Harleston "Edwin Harleston") (1930), featured in the _Harlem Renaissance and Transatlantic Modernism_ exhibition at the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art")

Aaron Douglas pioneered the African-American modernist movement by combining aesthetic with ancient African traditional art. He set the stage for future African-American artists to utilize elements of African and African-American history alongside racial themes present in society.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:12-11)

In 2007, the [Spencer Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Museum_of_Art "Spencer Museum of Art") organized an exhibition titled _Aaron Douglas: African-American Modernist_. It was held in [Lawrence, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Kansas "Lawrence, Kansas"), at the Spencer Museum of Art between September 8 to December 2, 2007, and traveled to the [Frist Center for the Visual Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frist_Center_for_the_Visual_Arts "Frist Center for the Visual Arts") in Nashville, Tennessee, from January 18 to April 13, 2008. It was then on display at the [Smithsonian American Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_American_Art_Museum "Smithsonian American Art Museum") in Washington, D.C,. between May 9 and August 3, 2008. Finally, it traveled to the [Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schomburg_Center_for_Research_in_Black_Culture "Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture") in New York, New York, from August 30 to November 30, 2008. An exhaustive catalog of this exhibition was put together through collaboration between Spencer Museum of Art and [The University of Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kansas "University of Kansas"), with the title _Aaron Douglas: African American Modernist_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:2-15)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-16)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1)

Douglas's work was featured in the 2015 exhibition _[We Speak: Black Artists in Philadelphia, 1920s-1970s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We\_Speak:\_Black\_Artists\_in\_Philadelphia,\_1920s-1970s "We Speak: Black Artists in Philadelphia, 1920s-1970s")_ at the [Woodmere Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodmere_Art_Museum "Woodmere Art Museum").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-Woodmere_Art_Museum-17)

In 2016, with the opening of the [National Museum of African American History and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_American_History_and_Culture "National Museum of African American History and Culture"), an archive of artworks created by or having to do with Aaron Douglas became available on their website. Users can access the full references of these pieces of art to determine the creation date, subject of the art, and its current residence.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-18)

## Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Douglas_(artist)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Style")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/4a/Lagos%2C_Nigeria_by_Aaron_Douglas.jpg/250px-Lagos%2C_Nigeria_by_Aaron_Douglas.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lagos,_Nigeria_by_Aaron_Douglas.jpg)

_Lagos, Nigeria_ (1956)

Aaron Douglas developed two art styles during his career: first as a traditional [portraitist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait "Portrait"), then as a [muralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural "Mural") and [illustrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustrator "Illustrator").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:0-1) Influenced by having worked with [Winold Reiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winold_Reiss "Winold Reiss"), Douglas incorporated African themes into his artwork to create a connection between Africans and African Americans. His work is described as being abstract, in that he portrayed the universality of the African-American people through song, dance, imagery and poetry.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) Through his murals and illustrations for various publications, he addressed social issues connected with race and segregation in the United States, and was one of the first African-American visual artists to utilize African-centered imagery.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:8-10)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:5-3)

His work features silhouettes of men and women, often in black and white.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8) His human depictions have characteristically flat shapes that are angular and long, with slits for eyes. Often, his female figures are drawn in a crouched position or moving as if they are dancing in a traditional African way.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) He adopted elements of West African masks and sculptures into his own art,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:12-11) with a technique that utilized [cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism") to simplify his figures into lines and planes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:11-6) He employed a narrow range of color, tone and value, most often using greens, browns, mauves, and blacks, with his human forms in darker shades of the present colors of the painting. He created emotional impact with subtle gradations of color, often using concentric circles to influence the viewer to focus on a specific part of the painting.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9)

His artwork is two-dimensional, and his human figures are faceless, allowing their forms to be symbolic and general, so as to create a sense of unity between Africans and African Americans.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:9-9) Douglas’ paintings include semitransparent silhouettes to portray the struggle of African Americans and their relative successes in various aspects of social life.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:6-8) His work is described as unique in creating a link between African Americans and their African ancestry through visual elements that are rooted in African art, and thus give the African-American experience a symbolic aesthetic.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12)

    *   _Let My People Go_, circa 1935–39
    *   _The Judgment Day_, created in 1939

*   Mural series commissioned in 1934 by the [Works Progress Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Works_Progress_Administration "Works Progress Administration").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Douglas_(artist)#cite_note-:10-12) The series consists of four murals; 
    *   _The Negro in an African Setting,_ depicts elements of African cultural dances and music to highlight the central heritage of African Americans.
    *   _Slavery through Reconstruction,_ depicts the contrast between the promise of emancipation and political shift in power post-Civil War and the disappointments of Reconstruction in the United States.
    *   _The Idyll of the Deep South,_ depicts the perseverance of African-American song and dance against the cruelty of lynching and other threats to African Americans in the United States.
    *   _Song of the Towers,_ depicts three events in United States history from an African-American lens, including the movement of African Americans towards the North in the 1910s, the rise of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, and the Great Depression in the 1930s.

**Carbone Smolan Agency** was an independent [branding agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branding_agency "Branding agency") that operated in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1976 – 2019.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-2) Its [proprietors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ownership "Ownership") Kenneth Carbone and Leslie Smolan were awarded the 2014 [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts")Gold medal for their achievements in corporate identity design, publishing, and strategy.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carbone_Smolan_Agency&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 18: Seated woman leaning on a chair back next to a man leaning against a wall](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Leslie_Smolan_and_Ken_Carbone.jpg/250px-Leslie_Smolan_and_Ken_Carbone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leslie_Smolan_and_Ken_Carbone.jpg)

Leslie Smolan and Ken Carbone

In 1976 Ken Carbone opened the New York office of the Canadian graphic design firm Gottschalk+Ash International.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-4) In 1977 he met and hired Leslie Smolan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3) Theirs was an expanded view of "graphic design" beyond its two-dimensional applications and embraced the range interdisciplinary communication practices including customer experience design, architectural graphics, branded environments, and packaging design.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-DesignObserver-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-6)

In 1980 Carbone and Smolan bought out their Canadian partners through a [leveraged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leverage_(finance) "Leverage (finance)")[buyout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyout "Buyout"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3) and renamed the company Carbone Smolan Agency.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-7) Carbone was creative director; Smolan was director of creative strategy. Company served many notable corporate and cultural brands including such organizations as [Musée du Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_du_Louvre "Musée du Louvre"), [Christie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christie's "Christie's"), [Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Oriental_Hotel_Group "Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group"), [Morgan Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3)[Boston Consulting Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Consulting_Group "Boston Consulting Group"), [Tapestry Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapestry_Inc "Tapestry Inc")., [Dale Carnegie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dale_Carnegie "Dale Carnegie"), [Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse"), [High Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Museum_of_Art "High Museum of Art"), [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") and [Chicago Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Symphony_Orchestra "Chicago Symphony Orchestra").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-11)

In December 1985 Carbone Smolan Agency presented its credentials for the “Signalétique du Grand Louvre,” the visitor information and signage program to complement the Louvre's visitors' entrance and underground plaza being designed by [I.M. Pei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.M._Pei "I.M. Pei"), creator of the [Louvre Pyramid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre_Pyramid "Louvre Pyramid").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-12) The [French government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_government "French government") awarded the New York-based Carbone Smolan Agency the signage project October 3, 1986.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-13) Introduced to the public in 1989, Carbone Smolan's visitor information and signage program was predicated on the Arrondissements of Paris plan and remained in place as of 2019.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-14)

In their report on the selection of Ken Carbone and Leslie Smolan as AIGA Medalists in 2014, AIGA journalist Angela Riechers noted, “In 1985 they won the commission—an honor for a relatively young studio. The project’s success and high visibility helped establish CSA as a studio of major importance in the larger design landscape.”[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-AIGAProfiles-15) It was featured in "Graphic Design Since 1950" by [Alliance Graphique Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Graphique_Internationale "Alliance Graphique Internationale") and [Communication Arts magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_Arts_(magazine) "Communication Arts (magazine)"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-16) and was recipient of the [Communication Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_Arts "Communication Arts") 1990 Award of Excellence.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the ensuing years, Carbone Smolan Agency has designed for numerous notable cultural institutions including [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA "AIGA"), MoMA (New York), [Jewish Museum (Manhattan)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Museum_(Manhattan) "Jewish Museum (Manhattan)"), [Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_Museum_of_Los_Angeles_County "Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County"), and [Brooklyn Botanic Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Botanic_Garden "Brooklyn Botanic Garden").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-17) CSA has 20 exhibits in the AIGA permanent archives.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-19)

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

**Carbone Smolan Agency** was an independent [branding agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branding_agency "Branding agency") that operated in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1976 – 2019.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-2) Its [proprietors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ownership "Ownership") Kenneth Carbone and Leslie Smolan were awarded the 2014 [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Graphic_Arts "American Institute of Graphic Arts")Gold medal for their achievements in corporate identity design, publishing, and strategy.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carbone_Smolan_Agency&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 18: Seated woman leaning on a chair back next to a man leaning against a wall](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Leslie_Smolan_and_Ken_Carbone.jpg/250px-Leslie_Smolan_and_Ken_Carbone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leslie_Smolan_and_Ken_Carbone.jpg)

Leslie Smolan and Ken Carbone

In 1976 Ken Carbone opened the New York office of the Canadian graphic design firm Gottschalk+Ash International.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-4) In 1977 he met and hired Leslie Smolan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3) Theirs was an expanded view of "graphic design" beyond its two-dimensional applications and embraced the range interdisciplinary communication practices including customer experience design, architectural graphics, branded environments, and packaging design.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-DesignObserver-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-6)

In 1980 Carbone and Smolan bought out their Canadian partners through a [leveraged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leverage_(finance) "Leverage (finance)")[buyout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyout "Buyout"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3) and renamed the company Carbone Smolan Agency.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-7) Carbone was creative director; Smolan was director of creative strategy. Company served many notable corporate and cultural brands including such organizations as [Musée du Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_du_Louvre "Musée du Louvre"), [Christie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christie's "Christie's"), [Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Oriental_Hotel_Group "Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group"), [Morgan Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-:0-3)[Boston Consulting Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Consulting_Group "Boston Consulting Group"), [Tapestry Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapestry_Inc "Tapestry Inc")., [Dale Carnegie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dale_Carnegie "Dale Carnegie"), [Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse"), [High Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Museum_of_Art "High Museum of Art"), [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") and [Chicago Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Symphony_Orchestra "Chicago Symphony Orchestra").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-11)

In December 1985 Carbone Smolan Agency presented its credentials for the “Signalétique du Grand Louvre,” the visitor information and signage program to complement the Louvre's visitors' entrance and underground plaza being designed by [I.M. Pei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.M._Pei "I.M. Pei"), creator of the [Louvre Pyramid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre_Pyramid "Louvre Pyramid").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-12) The [French government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_government "French government") awarded the New York-based Carbone Smolan Agency the signage project October 3, 1986.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-13) Introduced to the public in 1989, Carbone Smolan's visitor information and signage program was predicated on the Arrondissements of Paris plan and remained in place as of 2019.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-14)

In their report on the selection of Ken Carbone and Leslie Smolan as AIGA Medalists in 2014, AIGA journalist Angela Riechers noted, “In 1985 they won the commission—an honor for a relatively young studio. The project’s success and high visibility helped establish CSA as a studio of major importance in the larger design landscape.”[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-AIGAProfiles-15) It was featured in "Graphic Design Since 1950" by [Alliance Graphique Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Graphique_Internationale "Alliance Graphique Internationale") and [Communication Arts magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_Arts_(magazine) "Communication Arts (magazine)"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-16) and was recipient of the [Communication Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_Arts "Communication Arts") 1990 Award of Excellence.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the ensuing years, Carbone Smolan Agency has designed for numerous notable cultural institutions including [AIGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIGA "AIGA"), MoMA (New York), [Jewish Museum (Manhattan)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Museum_(Manhattan) "Jewish Museum (Manhattan)"), [Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_Museum_of_Los_Angeles_County "Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County"), and [Brooklyn Botanic Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Botanic_Garden "Brooklyn Botanic Garden").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-17) CSA has 20 exhibits in the AIGA permanent archives.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carbone#cite_note-19)
